speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, you are supposed to pose the question and allow the officeholder to respond.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I can talk more about the context of the question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have actually posed a question to the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If there is a Parliamentary Question (PQ), it will be posed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As a response, if you have a supplementary question, you can pose after that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, can you please sit down and allow them to respond, please?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, Members may recall the case relating to Pi Jiapeng and Pansuk Siriwipa.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The couple was involved in a series of alleged cheating cases involving luxury goods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They fled Singapore last year, in 2022, while investigations were ongoing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such disclosure has to be weighed against possible prejudice to the individuals concerned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A case in point would be where, following the judgment of the High Court in Parti Liyani’s case in 2020, the Police commenced investigations against her employer’s son, Karl Liew, based on the High Court’s observations that he had given dishonest evidence under oath.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I informed this House of those investigations during the debates relating to the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, this does not mean that Police will automatically publish the names of the individuals under investigations, if their names had been made public in other, earlier proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The context in which the names had been published in other proceedings, the nature of those proceedings, the nature of the offences being investigated and the connection of the offences under investigations to the original proceedings and whether the agencies have taken the view that subsequent criminal proceedings are or are not possible – all of these are relevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An assessment of all the facts and the context has to be made, in considering the public interest, as to whether to disclose the names.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yet another type of example, where names have been published, is the case of Chew Eng Han.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was then arrested when attempting to flee Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police made public the arrest on the day he and his accomplices were arrested, and their identities were released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After investigations, Chew and one accomplice were charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Alex Yeung stated publicly that his passport had been impounded, in respect of some conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police then issued a media statement explaining that Yeung was assisting the Police but had not been arrested.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A fifth example would be where Police are investigating a case and there is a lot of misinformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police might then make public the accurate facts relating to the case to dispel the falsehoods – and we have done that in the past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As can be seen, there are a wide variety of situations where it may become necessary to make public the fact that a person is under investigation, has been arrested or is assisting in investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to assess the facts and the public interest involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The discussions surrounding No 38 Oxley Road are of significant public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One might say they are of at least as much interest as in the case of Parti Liyani, if the two can even be compared.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Oxley Road matter was debated extensively in this House, following the Ministerial Statements on the subject.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The findings by the Disciplinary Tribunal (DT) and the Court of Three Judges, in the disciplinary proceedings against Mrs Lee Suet Fern, and their findings on Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern are matters of public record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Both the DT and the Court of Three Judges found that Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern had lied under oath.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And let me remind Members of what both tribunals said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Three Judges said that Mrs Lee Suet Fern lied under oath, and I quote: (a) “... e agree with and affirm the DT’s finding that Mr Lee Hsien Yang was not telling the truth when he said that he was the one who had forwarded the draft last will to the respondent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the same reasons, we also agree with and affirm the DT’s findings that the respondent’s evidence on this issue, which echoed Mr Lee Hsien Yang's, was similarly untrue and to be rejected."; (b) The respondent also claimed in her Affidavit of Evidence-in-Chief (AEIC) that after she received a draft last will from Mr Lee Hsien Yang...she did not even open it...  e agree with the DT that it is implausible and ultimately incredible..."; (c)  e note that after the disciplinary proceedings were initiated, the respondent adopted the position, which the DT rejected and which we too have rejected as false..."; (d)  he respondent did act with a degree of dishonesty in the disciplinary proceedings..." Mr Lee Hsien Yang lied under oath – "...Mr Lee Hsien Yang was not telling the truth..." If you go to what the DT said at various parts: (a) "In essence, an elaborate edifice of lies was presented, both on oath (through Mr Lee Hsien Yang and the respondent’s affidavits and on the witness stand), and through their public and other statements (which were referred to and relied upon during the disciplinary proceedings).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The affidavits were contrived to present a false picture.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Several of the lies were quite blatant." (b) "Considered in totality, the respondent’s conduct was quite dishonest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang's and her conduct demonstrated a calculated attempt to: (i) ensure that Mr Lee executed the last will as quickly as possible without due regard for Mr Lee’s wishes, and (ii) hide their wrongdoing in having done so." (c) "Having procured the last will through these improper means, she and Mr Lee Hsien Yang then fabricated a series of lies and inaccuracies, to perpetuate the falsehood that Mrs Kwa Kim Lee had been involved in the last will, and hide their own role in getting Mr Lee to sign the last will and their wrongdoings..." (d) Mr Lee Hsien Yang and the respondent tried to explain away their conduct...

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their explanations ranged from the improbable to the patently contrived to the downright dishonest." (e) "The respondent was a deceitful witness...

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before us, she lied or became evasive whenever she thought it was to her benefit to lie or evade.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang’s conduct was equally deceitful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He lied to the public, he lied to the Ministerial Committee, and he lied to us...

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He had no qualms about making up evidence as he went along.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We found him to be cynical about telling the truth." (f) "...In plain language, the effect of what they said is this: Mr Lee Hsien Yang may make untrue statements in public and in private whenever there is no legal penalty for telling untruths.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His public and private statements cannot be relied upon to be accurate...

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not find their explanations credible." (g) "Mr Lee Hsien Yang’s explanations for the untruths in his posts were not credible...Mr Lee Hsien Yang knew the true facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He admitted that some of his statements were inaccurate." (h) "Mr Lee Hsien Yang lied to the public about how the last will was drafted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He admitted to us that some of his statements were inaccurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said his public statements could be inaccurate because they are not sworn statements and thus, he may not look at them carefully...

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was dishonest." The DT in essence said that Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern had combined to mislead and cheat the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police did not make public at that time in October 2021, that the couple was being investigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A question was asked in this House earlier this month, about some public statements which had been made relating to Oxley and the judgments of the DT and the Court of Three Judges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can look up the Question and Answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Question required discussing the accuracy of those public statements in the context of the judgments of the DT and the Court of Three Judges, and it required dealing with the honesty or otherwise of Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That there were ongoing Police investigations, arising from the findings of the DT and the Court of Three Judges, was in that context relevant and necessary to be disclosed, to give an accurate and full Answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was also accurate to give a complete answer to mention that Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern had not cooperated with the Police investigations after saying that they would.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reasons for disclosing that Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern were under investigation, are broadly similar to the reasons why it was disclosed that Mr Karl Liew was being investigated for perjury.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Mr Karl Liew’s case, we were discussing his conduct and the conduct of other family members and the Court’s findings in this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We thought it necessary to disclose in that context that Mr Karl Liew was being investigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He cooperated with the investigation; he has since been charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Members may also recall – that I had said in this House when we were discussing the Parti Liyani case, that if any judgment or decision issued in the course of any legal proceedings contains findings, that there may have been perjury or other serious offences, that is something that we will take seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not recall any Member expressing a different view, that such lying on oath in Court proceedings should not be taken seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was the situation with Mr Karl Liew, and that is the situation with Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I said, with the added fact that they have also absconded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had been found to be dishonest and more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And those facts were disclosed so that this House can have a full and complete picture, when a question had been asked which related to their conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we cannot or should not answer the question in part or full, then, we would also have said so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In deciding whether we make public that investigations are ongoing, one factor which is considered is prejudice to the person being investigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether names should be released in a particular situation is a matter of judgment on what public interest requires.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The examples I gave earlier illustrate the exceptions when names were made public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if you take the case of Mr Karl Liew, what is the prejudice to him?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Mr Karl Liew’s case, the High Court had taken the view that he was not telling the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The same applies to Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members who are not lawyers may not know this but when a DT says that a person is guilty, it can only do so if it is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt on the guilt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise for the Court of Three Judges in disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The statements in Parliament about Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern do not materially add to any cloud the couple may already be under based on what the DT and the Court of Three Judges have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the facts are different, then the position will be different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, say a name had been published in other proceedings and the Court had made some findings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if our agencies are not able to prosecute the individual based on the earlier Court findings – because they assess that despite the earlier Court findings, substantial new facts have to be proven and that relevant evidence is not available and that relevant witnesses are not available, then there can be arguments both ways, on disclosure, and an assessment has to be made on the specific facts and a judgment has to be made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the cases of Mr Liew, and the Lees are quite different; and as I have said in the case of the Lees, they have also absconded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can tell Members that there is another case where the highest Court had made observations that a couple of persons had lied on oath.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a relevant question or issue about that matter, I can see that we will also set out the facts and say that Police are investigating.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But just like with Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern initially, when investigations had first commenced, Police had not volunteered the information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Police will respond with the facts if there is a need to – for example, if questions are raised in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee Suet Fern will have every right to provide explanations, on the matters being investigated if they eventually decide to do the right thing and cooperate with the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is their choice whether they want to be fugitives from justice, or whether they come and explain why they say the Courts were wrong to say that they had lied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The case of Keppel Offshore & Marine Limited (KOM) is quite different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not fall within the different examples I have set out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may not know this, but it was KOM which had made the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We received some information from Brazil, but it was not adequate to mount any criminal charge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were no admissions which could be relied upon to cross the evidentiary requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The documents between the US authorities and KOM and the DPA, also do not meet the evidentiary requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They go some way, but they do not cross the threshold in respect of those who were being investigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The CPIB, for good reasons, has the reputation for being able to ferret out the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But even the CPIB cannot get something out or proceed with charges when there are no documents or other evidence which cross the evidential threshold, and which can be used to break down the interviewees’ defences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, if any Member feels that this general policy should be changed and that law enforcement agencies should name all individuals who are being investigated, regardless of the circumstances and even if they are not abscondees from jurisdiction, and even if no charges are likely to brought in the end, then please let me know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would be surprised if anyone says that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If everyone agrees that persons under investigations should in general not be named, then the only question is the circumstances under which nevertheless names will be disclosed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have explained some examples of when names have been disclosed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact that no one raised any issues with Mr Liew being named, or when names of other abscondees had been disclosed, shows that no one in this House took issue with this disclosure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I thank the Minister for the explanation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can you keep it to two supplementary questions so that others can ask as well?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will come back to you if there is time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The issue here is really about fairness before the law whether we have the rule of law in Singapore or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister has shared that some of the exceptions involve the offender having absconded.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But is the KOM case not also a matter of very wide public interest?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: A lot of people are very interested in the names of the six individuals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not understand the legal process very well but under the stern warning letter, is there a paragraph that says that these six individuals of KOM are guilty but the prosecutor decided or the CPIB decided not to pursue the case because of some other reasons.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we have a situation here that for a KOM case – actually it is a more serious case – they are actually guilty and we have the names in the foreign jurisdiction documents already – this is one point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second point is that the KOM case is actually of deep public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I understand the Member, he says that the KOM case is a case of public interest, people are interested to know their names, so why is there a double standard?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Did the Member listen to the explanation on the difference between the KOM case and the case of the Lees and Mr Liew?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perhaps the Member can go into a little bit of detail, based on the explanation I have given on the differences and tell us, which part of the explanation he disagrees with before he alleges double standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Get to the facts, I have set out what the differences are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tell me which part the Member does not understand or disagrees with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, for the record, I have made it very clear why the disclosure here is consistent with the disclosure in the Karl Liew's case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Sir, through you, I would also like to ask Mr Leong, if Mr Leong did not see any problem when Mr Liew's name was mentioned in similar circumstances – in fact, he took part in the debate and wanted a commission of inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why then this extraordinary concern suddenly about the Lees that he did not show for Mr Liew?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And perhaps he can explain why his approach shows double standards?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I asked you a question and you framed it in a different context —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, Mr Leong, if you can address it through me and lower the temperature.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, he addressed it in a different context and then asked me a question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Did the Police issue a written order to Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Ms Lee Suet Fern?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just one supplementary question on the general principle behind when these disclosures of ongoing investigations are made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When the Government decides that it is in the public interest to make a disclosure about an ongoing investigation, what are the safeguards put in place to make sure that that disclosure into the public domain does not prejudice in some way the conduct of due process and subsequent trial and so on that may happen later on?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, one could say that that is the key point in making a decision on going public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is why you need to look carefully at the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you look at the facts relating to Mr Liew and the Lees, what has happened?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court has said that, in the case of Mr Liew, perhaps in less clear language; in the case of the Lees, very direct language, which I have taken you through – that at least Mr Liew as well as the two Lees were not telling the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the other aspect of prejudice that people will think less well of them the fact that we repeat in this House what the Courts have already said about them, is not going to increase the cloud as it were.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these are factors in the prejudice that you should take into account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Both the legal prejudice of fair trial as well as public perception prejudice, you should consider even before you release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not try and recover ground after that and shore up as it were.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is an assessment and it is an assessment we have to make.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, in the case of the Lees, I have explained why I think the prejudice is pretty much non-existent because we are simply repeating what has been said and saying that the Police are investigating that matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which everyone would expect us to do anyway, because I have said in this House we will investigate these matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But there may be other cases potentially where the prejudice could be a little bit more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have to assess public interest and that is why we have Parliament and when somebody takes a different view on prejudice, we will have to answer the questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they will obviously be entitled to their full rights to give their version of events and they will be entitled to defend their position in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have one supplementary question for the Minister to aid understanding of what he said earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I think the question was posed to him by Mr Leong about whether the Police had actually issued an order to Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Mrs Lee to attend the interview.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And his answer was that they were emailed, and they said that they would cooperate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do I read from that that actually, the Police had not gotten to the stage when an order under the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) was actually issued to them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police normally would not issue such an order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They would first contact, then speak with and then send the written document.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if a party says that they will cooperate, the Police would assume in good faith that that is how they will proceed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what was done and the next thing the Police heard was another email from the couple saying that they will not cooperate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But by then, they had already – as I said – essentially absconded from jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister mentioned that the Disciplinary Tribunal (DT) and the Court of Three Judges have found them guilty of lying under oath.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But exactly what lies these are, were not mentioned.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister share with us what exactly are the lies they were found to have said?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister like to clarify on the situation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The relevant extracts are also in Senior Minister Teo's answer as an Annex.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we give answers in Parliament, we expect Members to read them, and I do not think we want to waste Parliament's time with me going through that again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the second point, can I invite the Member to make it clear?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is the Member suggesting that there is a connection between the Bloomberg interview and the disclosure in Parliament?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because we do not repeat rumours from outside.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: No, I am not suggesting that, but I am aware that there are such speculations going on and it is quite prevalent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, I am merely asking if the Minister would like to take this opportunity to clarify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is not being suggested, then I would ask, Sir, through you, that the Member withdraw that part of her question and I would answer the rest of the question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any further questions, Ms Hazel Poa?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are many rumours swirling about outside on many other issues.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If that is the situation, then I would withdraw the question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And therefore, even the prescience of this Government could not have foretold that Mr Lee Hsien Yang was going to give such an interview.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I stand corrected, but that is my recollection of the sequence of events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if a question is asked in Parliament, we answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The debate for us is, I have explained the reasons why the answer was given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one took issue when I disclosed that Mr Liew was being investigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume that everyone accepted the principle and I have explained how that principle applies here.
